task_row_model.query: For multi-shell diffusion MRI datasets, what preprocessing and response-function estimation steps are recommended to minimize spurious fibre-orientation peaks in constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD) at crossings, and how should spherical harmonic order (lmax) and regularization be adapted across shells of differing b-value and SNR?

documents.content: Functional MRI preprocessing focuses on temporal and physiological confounds rather than microstructural orientation estimation. Typical steps include slice-timing correction, motion correction with realignment, spatial smoothing, and GLM-based denoising using motion regressors and physiological noise models. Temporal filtering and artifact detection (e.g., ICA-based removal) are applied prior to first-level modeling. fMRI pipelines do not estimate diffusion response functions or spherical harmonic representations of orientation distributions; their spatial smoothing and temporal processing choices are geared to BOLD signals and hemodynamic modeling rather than diffusion-weighted contrast.

Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) characterizes voxelwise Gaussian diffusion using the diffusion tensor to derive scalar maps such as fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), axial and radial diffusivities. Tensor estimation requires robust fitting to the diffusion-weighted signal, often with outlier rejection and motion correction. While DTI captures principal diffusion direction in single-fiber regions, it cannot resolve complex crossing geometries reliably; higher-order models like CSD or multi-compartment reconstructions are needed for resolving multiple orientations within a voxel. DTI-focused literature emphasizes eigenvector stability and tensor-derived tractography limitations.

A practical pipeline to reduce spurious CSD peaks combines careful preprocessing, robust response estimation, and shell-aware parameter choices. Preprocess with MP-PCA denoising, Gibbs ringing removal, susceptibility correction with topup, eddy/motion correction with slice-to-volume options, bias-field correction (N4) and correct gradient rotations and brain masking. Use unsupervised or semi-supervised response estimation that selects single-fiber WM voxels per shell and isolates isotropic GM/CSF responses (e.g., Dhollander-style). For multi-shell multi-tissue CSD, estimate per-tissue, per-shell response amplitudes and perform intensity normalization across shells. Set lmax in accordance with b-value and SNR (lower lmax for b<=1000, moderate for 1000–2500, higher for >2500); consider using consistent lmax for MSMT but stronger regularization on low-b/low-SNR shells. Enforce non-negativity, apply modest Laplacian or Tikhonov smoothing tuned by QC, and use amplitude and angular criteria for peak acceptance to eliminate spurious orientations.

Preprocessing has an outsized effect on downstream CSD quality. Begin with noise reduction (MP-PCA) to improve SNR, then remove Gibbs ringing to avoid edge-induced artifacts. Susceptibility-induced distortions should be corrected with a fieldmap or paired phase-encode (topup) acquisition; eddy current and motion distortion correction must follow, with careful rotation of diffusion gradient vectors. Finally, perform bias-field correction and obtain a tight brain mask. Many false peaks arise from residual motion, inter-shell intensity mismatch, and insufficient denoising, so iterate preprocessing and visually inspect spherical harmonic reconstructions for artifacts before response estimation.

Multi-tissue CSD models the diffusion signal as a mixture of anisotropic white-matter and isotropic compartments for grey matter and CSF. Conceptually, separating isotropic contributions reduces the background that can create spurious lobes in the fibre orientation distribution. The method estimates tissue-specific response functions and deconvolves the observed signal into a common FOD for white matter plus isotropic scalars. Theoretical work emphasizes identifiability of compartments given sufficient shell diversity; practical success depends on robust voxel selection for pure tissue responses and on regularization choices during spherical deconvolution.
